Learning Objectives
Review the normal anatomy and physiology of the labrum and the proximal biceps tendon.
Discuss the pathophysiology of superior labrum anterior to posterior tears and proximal
biceps lesions.
Identify clinical and imaging diagnostic methods for superior labrum anterior to posterior tears
and proximal biceps lesions.
Create appropriate treatment regimens for superior labrum anterior to posterior tears and
proximal biceps lesions.

Overview
A superior labrum anterior to posterior (SLAP) lesion is a detachment of the superior portion
of the glenoid labrum, including the anterior and posterior aspects.
The long head of the biceps brachii tendon at its insertion may or may not be involved.
This injury typically occurs in patients who perform repetitive overhead activities, such as
overhead athletes, but also may occur in patients who sustain acute trauma.
Epidemiology
The true incidence, age distribution, and sex distribution of SLAP tears depend heavily on
three factors:
Definition of a SLAP tear
Inclusion of degenerative labral pathology
Exclusion of associated pathologies, such as glenohumeral osteoarthritis or rotator cuff tear
Isolated clinically important SLAP tears often occur in young overhead and throwing athletes.
SLAP tears may be associated with episodes of shoulder instability, especially in athletes.
Patients undergoing SLAP tear repair are more likely to be male and historically in their
twenties or forties; however, the indications for SLAP repair are being refined.
In throwing athletes, SLAP repair rather than biceps tenodesis is the preferred treatment
option.
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Structural Anatomy
The glenoid labrum consists of parallel collagen fibers that course around the circumference of
the glenoid.
The superior labrum inserts on the superior glenoid rim, medial to the articular cartilage
margin, through a transitional zone of fibrocartilage.
A normal synovial recess exists between the meniscoid or triangular superior labrum and the
articular cartilage extension over the superior glenoid rim.
The supraglenoid tubercle may serve as the sole or combined (in combination with the
superior labrum) origin of the long head of the biceps tendon.
The long head of the biceps origin often is preferentially or entirely posterior in reference to
the vertical axis of the glenoid.

The biceps tendon is an intra-articular but extra-synovial structure within the glenohumeral
joint.
Passes through the bicipital groove, or intertubercular groove, between the greater and
lesser tuberosities
Stability of the biceps within this region is afforded by the biceps sling, or pulley, consisting of
fibers from the following:
Subscapularis tendon
Supraspinatus tendon
Coracohumeral ligament
Superior glenohumeral ligament
Medial subluxation of the biceps tendon should increase concern for a clinically important
subscapularis tear.
The superior labrum/biceps anchor complex serves as a secondary restraint to anterior
translation in abduction and external rotation.
The long head of the biceps brachii
Static humeral head depressor
Secondary stabilizer to anterior and posterior translation
Not shown to serve an important dynamic role in glenohumeral joint kinematics or stability
(Resource 1).

Structural Anatomy
The glenohumeral joint lacks bony constraint with a shallow glenoid socket. The labrum
deepens the glenoid by 100%. This enhances glenohumeral joint stability by increasing
the surface area of the glenoid. The labrum also serves as an attachment site for the
glenohumeral ligaments.
Vasculature
Vascularity to the glenoid labrum originates from the scapular, circumflex scapular, and
posterior circumflex humeral arteries via capsular or periosteal vessels (Figure 1).
Vascularity of the long head of the biceps tendon

Primarily provided by the ascending branch of the anterior humeral circumflex artery, which
travels within the bicipital groove.
An avascular zone exists at its proximal portion, close to the superior glenoid.
Figure 1 Histologic coronal section of the glenohumeral joint shows the capsular and periosteal
contributions to the vascularity of the labrum and the meniscoid superior labrum and the
synovial recess created by the articular cartilage extension beyond the superior glenoid rim. C =
capsular contributions, P = periosteal contributions. (Reproduced with permission from Cooper
DE, Arnoczky SP, O’Brien S, Warren RF, DiCarlo E, Allen AA: Anatomy, histology, and vascularity of
the glenoid labrum: An anatomical study. J Bone Joint Surg Am 1992;74[1]:46-52.)
Nerves
The glenoid labrum and surrounding capsule are innervated.
Histologic analysis has shown mechanoreceptors that likely respond to compressive force.
Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
Various mechanisms of injury have been described in the pathogenesis of superior labrum
tears.
Direct traction to the biceps tendon

Internal impingement
Peel-back
May be the primary mechanism in throwers
With the shoulder in abduction and external rotation, the orientation and pull of the biceps
pulls the labrum off the posterosuperior glenoid.
Internal impingement and peel-back may be exacerbated by posterior capsule contracture.
Unique aspects of glenohumeral joint kinematics in the throwing athlete are relevant to the
etiology of superior labrum tears.
Contracture of the posterior band of the inferior glenohumeral ligament exerts a posterior
force on the ligament, which tethers the humeral head and shifts the glenohumeral contact
point posterosuperiorly in composite abduction and external rotation.
This posterosuperior shift allows for hyperexternal rotation at the glenohumeral joint by
avoiding abutment of the greater tuberosity against the posterosuperior glenoid and by
increasing the redundancy of the anteroinferior capsule.
This posterosuperior shift in the humeral head with resultant hyperexternal rotation
accounts for the exacerbation of internal impingement of the rotator cuff on the
posterosuperior labrum and the peel-back mechanism of superior labrum tears.
Associated Injuries
SLAP tears frequently are identified in combination with other pathologic features.
The presence of concomitant injuries is highly dependent on the mechanism of injury and 
patient demographics.
After a first-time dislocation, identification of a SLAP tear is not atypical.
In an analysis of SLAP tears, Snyder et al1; reported the following:
Of the patients studied, 40% had an associated rotator cuff tear and 22% had an associated
Bankart lesion.
Study population characteristics
Predominantly male
Aged 16 to 73 years (mean age, 38 years)
Wide range of professions
Injury Classification
SLAP tears are classified into 10 types (Table 1).

The original classification of SLAP tears consisted of four types:
Type I: degenerative fraying with an intact biceps anchor (Figure 2, A)
Type II: unstable biceps anchor detached from the underlying glenoid (Figure 2, B)
Type IIa: anterosuperior
Type IIb: posterosuperior
Type IIc: combined anterior and posterior
Type III: bucket-handle tear with an intact biceps anchor (Figure 2, C)
Type IV: bucket-handle tear with extension into the biceps tendon (Figure 2, D)
The classification system was later expanded to include types V through X (Table 1).
Surgeons must recognize normal anatomic variants of the anterosuperior labrum on
diagnostic imaging studies and arthroscopy that are not pathologic and should not be
repaired.
Anterior sublabral foramen
Anterior sublabral foramen with cordlike middle glenohumeral ligament
Absent anterosuperior labrum with cordlike middle glenohumeral ligament (Buford complex)
Biceps anchor laxity with an intact anchor and inability to peel the superior biceps/labral
complex fully off the superior glenoid
Classification of biceps tendon pathology typically is descriptive.
Tear versus synovitis
Extent of tear based on percentage of the entire tendon
Location of pathology
Presence of subluxation or dislocation of the biceps from the bicipital groove

Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History

A history of acute trauma, consisting of sudden traction or compression to the affected
extremity, may be reported.
SLAP tears may be associated with a previous subluxation or dislocation event.
An insidious onset of symptoms associated with SLAP tears is most common in overhead
throwing athletes.
Pain caused by a SLAP tear often is localized deep within the glenohumeral joint and may be
associated with mechanical symptoms, fatigue or a dead arm sensation of the extremity
during overhead activities, or frank weakness of the rotator cuff in a concomitant paralabral
cyst.
Physical Examination
Provocative Testing
Various provocative tests have been described for SLAP tears and biceps pathology; however,
none are of sufficient accuracy to confirm the diagnosis.
O’Brien Active Compression Test

O'Brien Active Compression Test
The affected extremity is positioned in 90° of forward elevation, slight adduction, and
maximum internal rotation. The patient performs resisted forward elevation. The test is
repeated in maximum external rotation. The test is positive if pain occurs deep within
the shoulder in maximum internal rotation and then improves with maximum external
rotation.
Crank Test

Crank Test

The affected extremity is elevated to 160° in the scapular plane. Axial force is applied to
the extremity as the humerus is passively rotated. The test is positive if pain, clicking, or
catching is reproduced.
Biceps Load I and II Tests

Biceps Load I and II Tests
The affected extremity is abducted to 90° to 120° and maximally externally rotated. The
forearm is maximally supinated, and the elbow is flexed against resistance. The test is
positive if pain or apprehension worsens with resisted elbow flexion.
Anterior Slide Test

Anterior Slide Test
The hand of the affected extremity is placed on the hip with the thumb posterior. One
hand of the examiner is placed on the elbow of the affected extremity, exerting a slight
anterior and axial force to the extremity. The patient is asked to resist this force to the
elbow. The test is positive if pain, a pop, or a click is reproduced.
Speed Test

Speed Test
The affected extremity is elevated to 90° in full supination with the elbow extended. The
patient resists downward pressure on the extremity by the examiner. The test is positive
if pain is experienced in the anterior shoulder or the glenohumeral joint. The Speed test
is associated with poor sensitivity, moderate specificity, and poor accuracy. Diagnostic

Dynamic Labral Shear Test

Dynamic Labral Shear Test
The affected arm is externally rotated and progressively abducted while horizontally
extended. The test is positive if a reproducible painful click deep in the shoulder in the
mid-arc of abduction is reproduced.
Yergason Test

Yergason Test
The affected extremity is adducted against the side with the elbow flexed to 90° in full
pronation. The patient then supinates against resistance. The test is positive if pain is
experienced in the bicipital groove or glenohumeral joint. The Yergason test is
associated with poor sensitivity, moderate specificity, and poor accuracy. Diagnostic
injection of local anesthetic with or without corticosteroid into the glenohumeral joint or
the bicipital groove may aid in confirming the diagnosis.
Other Assessments
Rotator cuff strength and infraspinatus atrophy to identify patients who may have
suprascapular nerve compression from a paralabral ganglion cyst
Instability examination
Assessment of throwing athletes includes the total arc of rotation to identify a glenohumeral
internal rotation deficit.
Imaging Studies

Radiography
Plain radiographs of the shoulder are necessary to ensure that the glenohumeral joint has
normal mechanical alignment, preserved articular cartilage, and no fractures.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
 Preferred imaging modality
Diagnostic accuracy may be improved by positioning the arm in abduction and external
rotation.
A recent systematic review and meta-analysis confirmed that magnetic resonance
arthrography improves the diagnostic accuracy of MRI with regard to the detection of a SLAP
tear.1-4

Magnetic Resonance Imaging
According to the literature, the diagnostic accuracy of MRI ranges widely. Overdiagnosis
of SLAP tears is common because normal anatomy may be misconstrued as pathologic.
Accurate diagnosis is predicated on clinical examination and concordant MRI findings
and cannot be confirmed until the time of surgery.
Ultrasonography
 May be useful in the dynamic assessment of the biceps tendon within its groove
Less costly alternative to MRI in detecting biceps tenosynovitis and rotator cuff pathology
Ultrasonographic evaluation of the superior labrum may be possible but is operator
dependent and not widely performed.
Differential Diagnosis

SLAP tears may be found in combination with many other injuries. The true source of
symptoms must not be ignored because of a radiographic finding of a SLAP tear. These
sources may include biceps tendinosis, early glenohumeral arthritis, internal
impingement, suprascapular neuropathy from a spinoglenoid notch cyst (Figure 3), and
rotator cuff pathology.
Figure 3 T1-weighted, coronal MRI of the shoulder showing posterior superior labral
tears associated with a spinoglenoid cyst. These cysts cause compression of the
suprascapular nerve, which manifests primarily as weakness of the infraspinatus and
results in weakness of external rotation.
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Indications
Nonsurgical management is the first line of treatment, especially in patients older than 30
years and those not performing overhead activities.
Techniques/Procedures

Injection of local anesthetic with corticosteroid into the glenohumeral joint or the bicipital
groove is diagnostic and potentially therapeutic.
Aspiration of the spinoglenoid notch cyst may be performed to manage suprascapular nerve
compression.
Physical therapy for superior labrum tears
Rotator cuff strengthening
Periscapular muscular strengthening
Posteroinferior capsular stretching
In combination with physical therapy and possibly glenohumeral injection, rest from inciting
activities, such as throwing, should be initiated.
Outcomes
In the general population, predictive factors for failed nonsurgical management include history
of trauma, a positive compression-rotation test, and participation in overhead sports.
In baseball players, failure of conservative management is associated with advanced age,
prolonged symptoms, pitching, presence of exostosis of the posterior band of the inferior
glenohumeral ligament (Bennett lesion), and presence of partial articular rotator cuff tear.
Surgical Management
Indications
Persistent pain and dysfunction despite months of appropriate nonsurgical management
indicate the need for surgical management.
Surgical Approaches
Diagnostic arthroscopy is essential to identify and manage any concomitant pathology. It also
is essential to classify the SLAP tear to aid in selecting appropriate surgical management
(Resource 2).
Management based on classification
Type I degenerative tears typically demonstrate fraying, with an intact biceps anchor.
Débridement alone is sufficient.
Type II tears are unstable because of involvement of the biceps anchor. Reattachment of the
labrum to the superior glenoid rim is indicated.

In patients older than 35 to 40 years, biceps tenodesis may be preferred over SLAP repair
because of concerns for complications, such as re-tear and excessive stiffness.
In throwing athletes with a type II SLAP tear, repair over biceps tenodesis is the preferred
treatment option.
Type III tears are managed via débridement of the unstable bucket-handle labral tear.
Type IV tears are managed according to the status of the torn biceps tendon.
If less than 25% to 50% of the biceps tendon is involved, the tear and its extension into the
tendon are débrided.
If 25% to 50% or more of the biceps tendon is involved, biceps tenodesis or tenotomy with
labral débridement or repair is indicated.
Technique
Portals
Viewing: typically a standard posterior viewing portal
Working
Anterosuperior and anteroinferior portals
Alternatively, the portal of Neviaser can be used to pass the shuttling device beneath the
labral tissue (1 cm medial to the acromion at its junction with the scapular spine and the
posterior border of the distal clavicle).
Anchor placement
Anterosuperior rotator interval portal—An accessory trans-rotator cuff posterolateral
portal can be used for anchors placed posterior to the biceps tendon.
The portal of Wilmington also has been described for this purpose (the clinician should
pierce the cuff at the myotendinous junction; Figure 4).

Postoperative rehabilitation depends on the surgical treatment option performed.
SLAP repair
Period of immobilization followed by progression of passive and active motion
Gradual, progressive range of motion protocol is initiated immediately.
Full range of motion should be achieved within the first 6 weeks postoperatively.
Patients should be protected from early abduction and external rotation positions.
Strengthening, beginning with the periscapular musculature and advancing to the rotator
cuff, typically begins at approximately 4 weeks postoperatively.
Slow return to full activity, including athletics, may begin at approximately 4 months
postoperatively. This should be a gradual return guided by pain in patients who have
recovered full range of motion.
Biceps tenodesis with labral débridement
Sling immobilization for 2 to 4 weeks postoperatively
Gradual return to activities, protecting the tenodesis for the first 6 weeks postoperatively,
should be encouraged.
Rehabilitation should be modified to account for the concomitant management of associated
pathology.
Complications
SLAP repair
Recurrent tear
Postoperative stiffness
Persistent pain
Biceps tenodesis
Biceps tendon rupture at the tenodesis site
Bicipital groove pain with proximal tenodesis
Biceps pain if the tendon is over-tensioned
Humeral fracture because of excessive reaming (rare)
Biceps tenotomy
Excessive cramping and pain
Subjective weakness of flexion or supination
Cosmetic deformity
Outcomes

Outcomes
Modern techniques and implants have been associated with favorable results with
regard to pain and return to function after SLAP repair. However, the ability to return to
sports activity is unpredictable and depends on the sport and position.
In the management of SLAP tears, some evidence shows that, compared with SLAP
repair, biceps tenodesis is associated with more favorable results and lower
complication rates and should be considered in less active patients or those older than
40 years. A recent systematic review and meta-analysis suggested an advantage of
biceps tenodesis with respect to patient satisfaction and return to sports activity.2
A recent double-blind, randomized controlled trial demonstrated no difference in
outcomes among sham surgery, SLAP repair, and biceps tenodesis4; (Videos 1, 2 and 3).
